description: Learn how to show or send your work. Choose a file type that fits the job. Check your facts and keep private details safe.

questionVariants: What changes when you share or publish finished work?
What do sharing and publishing let your audience do?
How does sharing finished work differ from keeping it to yourself?
answerVariants: The chosen people can access the completed work.
The intended audience can see the finished design.
Other people are given access to the finished work.

concepts.conceptName: Choose Who Should See the Work
questionVariants: What should you decide first before sharing?
What is the first audience question before you send a design?
Before you give access, what should you know?
answerVariants: Who is supposed to see the work.
Which people should receive it.
The people the work is meant for.

questionVariants: Must a finished school project be public?
Does completing your work mean everyone should see it?
Should every completed class design go on the open web?
answerVariants: No. It may be just for the teacher or class.
No. Only the chosen audience may need it.
No. It can stay within the approved group.

questionVariants: What does presentation mode do?
Which view helps you show slides during a talk?
How can you show your slides without the editing workspace?
answerVariants: It shows slides to the audience with editing tools out of view.
It displays the slides and hides the editor controls.
It gives a clear slide view without the editing tools.

questionVariants: What does printing a design do?
How can you turn a design into a sign for a door?
Which output makes a paper handout?
answerVariants: It puts the design on paper.
It makes a paper copy.
It creates a physical page you can hand out or display.

concepts.conceptName: Save a Copy in a Chosen File Type
questionVariants: What do download and export let you create?
What do you get when you download or export a project?
How do download and export differ from giving people access?
answerVariants: A saved file copy in a chosen format.
A copy saved as the type of file you choose.
An output file in a chosen type, saved to your device.

questionVariants: What is a file format?
What do names like PNG, JPG, and PDF tell you?
What does a file's format describe?
answerVariants: The type of file and how its information is stored.
The kind of file used to store the work.
The way the file stores its digital information.

questionVariants: What is PNG often useful for?
When is PNG a useful output choice?
What kind of work often fits a PNG file?
answerVariants: Graphics, screenshots, or a page saved as a picture.
A graphic or screenshot that needs to be an image.
A finished graphic, text design, or screenshot as an image.

questionVariants: What is JPG often used for?
What kind of page often suits a JPEG file?
When might JPG be a useful image format?
answerVariants: Photos or pages made mostly of photographs.
A photograph or a photo-heavy design.
An image that is mostly a photo.

questionVariants: What is PDF useful for?
Which job does a PDF file often do well?
Why might a teacher ask for a handout as a PDF?
answerVariants: It keeps a document's layout together for reading or printing.
It preserves where things sit on a document page.
It helps a document keep its page layout across devices.

concepts.conceptName: Choose a File Type for the Job
questionVariants: How should you choose an output format?
Is the largest file always the best choice?
What should guide your choice of file type?
answerVariants: Choose the type that fits the task and teacher directions.
Use the format needed for the job, not just the largest one.
Match the file type to its use and the class directions.

questionVariants: Which three actions can permissions control?
Which three kinds of access do permission settings cover?
What three things might a project let other people do?
answerVariants: Whether people may view, comment, or change the work.
Whether others can look, leave notes, or make changes.
Who may see it, add feedback, or alter the project.

questionVariants: What can someone do with view-only access?
What does viewing permission allow?
A partner has view-only permission. What can they do?
answerVariants: See the work without changing it.
Look at the design but leave it as it is.
Open and read it, but not alter the design.

questionVariants: What is comment access for?
What does commenting permission let a partner add?
How can someone give feedback with comment access?
answerVariants: They can leave notes about the work.
They may add feedback without changing the design itself.
They can write suggestions beside the project.

questionVariants: What can someone do with edit access?
What does editing permission let a partner do?
Why does edit access need care?
answerVariants: They can change the project itself.
They may alter its words, pictures, or layout.
They can make changes to the design.

questionVariants: A partner only needs to look. Which access is enough?
Should a reader get permission to change your work?
What permission fits someone who only needs to see a poster?
answerVariants: View-only access is enough.
Let them view, without edit access.
Give viewing permission, following teacher directions.

questionVariants: A classmate asks you to make a public link. What comes first?
What should you do before changing who can access class work?
How should you choose a way to send school work?
answerVariants: Ask the teacher and follow the approved class method.
Use the teacher's directions for sharing.
Check with your teacher and use the allowed method.

concepts.conceptName: Links Can Travel Beyond the Class
questionVariants: Why can an anyone-with-the-link setting be risky?
Why should a school link not be sent to just anyone?
What can happen when a public project link is passed around?
answerVariants: People outside the intended group may get access.
The work may reach people it was not meant for.
Someone may pass it to unapproved viewers.

questionVariants: Which details need a privacy check before sharing?
What information about students should make you stop and ask?
What personal details should you check before you publish?
answerVariants: Names, faces, places, and contact details.
Student names, photos, locations, and ways to contact them.
Details that identify people, such as faces or addresses.

questionVariants: What belongs in the final content check?
What should you proofread before sending an event poster?
How do you check whether a finished poster says the right things?
answerVariants: Check facts, dates, spelling, and required credits.
Make sure facts, labels, dates, and credits are correct.
Review facts, spelling, names, dates, and needed source credit.

questionVariants: What belongs in the final design check?
Which visual parts belong in the design check?
What does the design part of the final checklist cover?
answerVariants: Check the main idea, readable words, useful pictures, and spacing.
Make sure the main idea is clear and the parts are well placed.
Review the clear message, text size, pictures, and arrangement.

questionVariants: What belongs in the final accessibility check?
How can you check the finished work for readers with different needs?
What should you check so more people can use the output?
answerVariants: Check contrast, non-color clues, reading order, and image descriptions.
Review light and dark contrast, extra clues, order, and picture descriptions.
Check that meaning uses more than color and that order and image descriptions work.

questionVariants: What belongs in the final privacy and permission check?
What should you review about access and allowed images before sending?
What does the privacy and permission part of the final checklist cover?
answerVariants: Check who gets it, private details, and allowed media use.
Review the audience, personal details, and image permissions.
Check the intended viewers, private information, and media rules.

questionVariants: What makes a useful school file name?
How should you name the final copy of a plant poster?
What helps a teacher identify a file without opening it?
answerVariants: A clear topic and stage, such as Plant_Poster_Final.
The topic and whether it is a draft or final copy.
A name that tells the project and version, without private details.

concepts.conceptName: Keep Important Parts Away from Edges
questionVariants: The printer cuts off words at the edge. What can help?
What should you try if a printed title loses its last letters?
How can you fix important parts that disappear at the page edge?
answerVariants: Move them inward and check page size and margins.
Leave more edge space and review the print settings.
Keep key parts away from the edge and check the page settings.

questionVariants: Why preview a print or exported file?
Why check a saved output even if the editor looked good?
Why test the actual version people will receive?
answerVariants: Size, colors, edges, or image clarity may look different.
The finished copy may look different from the editing view.
Things can change when work moves from screen to final output.

questionVariants: How much writing belongs on a slide for a talk?
How can you fix a slide full of report paragraphs?
What should a slide show while you explain the details aloud?
answerVariants: One main idea with short phrases and useful pictures.
Keep the key idea, a few words, and helpful images.
Use a clear main point, brief words, and visuals.

questionVariants: What should you do while showing a slide?
How should you speak about the picture on your screen?
What helps you present instead of reading every word aloud?
answerVariants: Face the audience and explain ideas in your own words.
Look toward the listeners and tell what the visuals mean.
Speak to the group and explain, rather than only reading the screen.
